claims.overstatement: Slight, one word: 'non-depressed'. The trial excluded current major depression (Methods > Recruitment; Limitations), but it does not describe participants as non-depressed, and their baseline CES-D averaged 20.2 (SD 8.8), which on the standard 20-item scale lies above the usual screening threshold of 16 (the threshold is general knowledge, not stated in the paper; the paper cites a short-version reference and does not say which version it used). 'Without current major depression' matches the source. Minor: the 24-week net RR 0.75 (0.56-1.00, p = .05) sits under the verb 'lowered'; the claim prints its interval, so the borderline result is visible.
claims.note: Scope of this check: coffin_2020 covers the second trial only. The first trial's figures (RR 0.57, 0.35-0.93; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63%; editors' RR 0.71, 0.42-1.18) are not reported in this source, which says only that its authors' prior 12-week trial in 60 men who have sex with men showed significant reductions; those numbers must be checked against colfax_2011. Second-trial numbers recomputed: week-12 positive samples 25/38 = 65.8% vs 32/41 = 78.0%; week 24 20/32 = 62.5% (printed 63%) vs 29/39 = 74.4%; week 36 25/35 = 71.4% vs 37/42 = 88.1%; all match. Modelled RRs 0.67 (0.51-0.87), 0.75 (0.56-1.00), 0.73 (0.57-0.96) match Table 2 and the abstract. End-of-study abstinence 11/60 = 18.3% vs 5/60 = 8.3%; crude OR from these counts is 2.47 (0.80-7.61): the printed interval reproduces exactly, and the printed point estimate 2.50 is evidently rounded (the paper gives 2.50 for weeks 12, 24 and 36; week 36 recomputes to 2.51, 0.62-10.21). NNT 1/0.10 = 10 at weeks 12 and 24 and 1/0.067 = 15 at week 36, as printed. Drowsiness 18/60 = 30% vs 6/60 = 10% (no test reported). WisePill adherence means 38.5% vs 39.5% (week 12) and 28.1% vs 38.5% (week 24), all below 50%. Editors' rough check (not a reproduction of the model): the raw sample-level ratios are about 0.84 (week 12), 0.84 (week 24) and 0.81 (week 36); dividing by the baseline ratio of urine positivity (85% vs 75%, 1.13) gives 0.74, 0.74 and 0.72, close to the modelled 0.67, 0.75 and 0.73. The modelled effect is therefore largely the mirtazapine arm's larger fall from a higher starting point, which is what a divergence-of-trends model estimates but is worth knowing when the claim sets 66% vs 78% beside RR 0.67. 'Lowered the modelled weekly probability' fairly describes the GEE log-link RR (divergence of fitted trends after accounting for the fitted baseline difference, week 1 omitted). On independence: the source's Key Points call the two studies '2 independent randomized clinical trials', while the Introduction and Discussion describe the first as the authors' own earlier 12-week trial by the same group, and two authors of this trial (G. Colfax, G.-M. Santos) are the first two authors of the prior trial (reference 30). Shared investigators, group and population are thus documented here; shared site and analysis model are not described for the first trial in this source.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'with no difference between the two drugs' rests on a non-significant test for subgroup differences (chi-square 0.29, df 1, p = 0.59) between three bupropion and two modafinil trials with wide intervals (modafinil OR 0.86, 0.46-1.61; bupropion 1.12, 0.54-2.33); 'neither drug differed from placebo, and the two did not differ detectably from each other' would match the source more exactly. Otherwise the wording is faithful and non-causal.
claims.note: Numbers recomputed. 70/353 = 19.8% and 62/289 = 21.5% (Table 2); 353 + 289 = 642. OR 0.97 (0.65-1.45), I2 2% (chi-square 4.08, df 4, p = 0.40), p = 0.87. Per 1,000: applying the pooled OR to the pooled placebo risk (62/289 = 215 per 1,000) gives -5.1 (-63.8 to +69.2), i.e. 5 fewer (64 fewer to 69 more), as printed in Tables 2 and 3. Retention: 332/626 = 53.0%, 268/558 = 48.0%; 626 + 558 = 1184; OR 1.20 (0.91-1.58), I2 15% (chi-square 15.34, df 13, p = 0.29); GRADE-style +45.5 (-23.5 to +113.2) per 1,000, printed as 46 more (23 fewer to 113 more). All match. Caution for the editor: '5 fewer per 1,000' is GRADE's model-based absolute effect, not the crude difference between the two percentages the claim also prints (19.8% - 21.5% = 1.6 points, 16 fewer per 1,000; crude OR 0.91); a reader setting the two side by side may see a mismatch. Same for retention (crude +50 per 1,000 vs GRADE +46). Not an error in the claim, but if both are shown the per-1,000 figure should be labelled as the summary-of-findings estimate. Other points the claim does not carry: (a) both outcomes are rated very low certainty by the authors (abstinence: risk of bias very serious, inconsistency serious, indirectness serious, imprecision very serious); (b) two of the five abstinence trials enrolled only people with non-daily use (low-frequency subgroup OR 1.24, 0.34-4.48, I2 74%); (c) the trials' own abstinence definitions differ in detail (e.g. Anderson 2015 counted at least two negative urines in weeks 11-12 as success, per Table 1), so 'urine-verified abstinence in the final two weeks' is the review's harmonised label; (d) for retention, a subgroup of two trials with more than 12 weeks of treatment (both methylphenidate, one in incarcerated men with ADHD) gave OR 2.45 (1.14-5.25), subgroup-difference p = 0.05, which the authors treat as hypothesis-generating; (e) a 151-participant bupropion trial (Elkashef 2008) entered neither analysis, excluded from retention for a stated sample overlap with Anderson 2015 that the review does not explain.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'Amineptine ... reduced discontinuation' states as a finding what the authors hedge (abstract: amineptine 'may reduce' discontinuation rates); the claim does attach 'very low certainty', so 'may have reduced' would match the source more closely. Nothing else overstated.
claims.note: Reading cautions (not errors): (a) 'no medication other than amineptine differed from placebo on any pooled outcome' is accurate, but the intervals are wide (any medication 0.40-1.23) and the authors say explicitly that the evidence cannot show the medications are ineffective; the claim does not say 'ineffective'. (b) Two of the six medications (ibudilast, varenicline) and one modafinil trial never entered a pooled outcome, so that sentence covers four medications; the magnitude's '6 trials, 186 participants' makes this visible. (c) Single trials outside the pooled outcomes did report differences from placebo (mirtazapine on withdrawal scores in one trial, amantadine on fatigue, varenicline on reaction time, ibudilast on 2 of 12 attention measures), so the restriction to 'pooled outcome' is doing real work. Numbers: every number in the statement and magnitude was found in Table 2 and reproduces exactly: discontinuation any medication RR 0.70 (0.40-1.23), 6 trials, 186 participants; mirtazapine 0.96 (0.48-1.92); modafinil 0.67 (0.22-2.03); amantadine 1.33 (0.34-5.24); amineptine 0.22 (0.07-0.72), very low; withdrawal SMD 0.17 (-0.43 to 0.77), 3 trials, 93; craving SMD 0.34 (-0.77 to 1.45), 2 trials, 48. Nine trials of six medications, six at high risk of bias, search to December 2020, market withdrawal in 1999 for liver toxicity and non-medical use, and one trial reporting adverse events by arm are all in the text. No editors' calculation in this claim. 'About 240 participants' is safe but the source is internally inconsistent: the text gives 242, the Table 1 rows sum to 241, and the arm counts given (129 on medication + 138 on placebo, with 48%/52%) sum to 267, presumably because crossover participants are counted in both arms. Section 3.5 says the discontinuation analysis had 188 people, Table 2 and Section 3.1 say 186 (89 medication, 97 placebo; Table 1 rows for the six trials also sum to 186). 'Two small trials by one group': the two amineptine trials (n = 30 and n = 44, both Thai inpatient settings) list the same three authors (references 51 and 54), so the statement is supported from the reference list, not from an explicit statement by the review. The 1999 market-withdrawal date is stated by the review in its Discussion citing two earlier case reports (1996 and 1998), so it is second-hand and the cited reports cannot themselves document a 1999 event; a primary regulatory source would be a better anchor for that sentence. Which six trials were at high risk of bias is shown only in Figure 2 (an image), so I could not check how many of the six pooled trials were high risk.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Results 3.1 says the search 'yielded 20 results', 11 of which did not meet the inclusion criteria (references 38-48, two of which, 43 and 47, are e-page conference-abstract citations). The text does not call the 20 'full texts'; that they were full-text assessments is a plausible inference, but the screening counts are only in the PRISMA figure (an image). Suggested wording: 'the search yielded 20 reports, 11 of which did not meet the criteria'. The rest of the finding (four databases to December 2020, ClinicalTrials.gov, reference lists, no language limits) is confirmed at Methods 2.3.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: NOT CHECKED on the registry side rather than absent: the PROSPERO record was not accessible in this session (no web access), so the planned odds ratios, planned time-period and subgroup analyses, English-language limit, database list and comorbidity exclusion could not be checked. Article side confirmed: the article calls the registration prospective (Methods 2.1), reports relative risks (2.8), states no language restriction (2.3), lists MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, EMBASE and ClinicalTrials.gov, reports no time-period or subgroup-by-setting analyses, and acknowledges no deviation from protocol. Treat the registry content of this item as single-reader.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument and the item judgments follow from the article. Items 11 (no investigation of heterogeneity up to I2 71%, inconsistent and partly invalid global-state effect measure) and 15 (publication bias neither assessed nor discussed; GRADE domains listed omit it) are each a critical 'no', so critically low confidence follows from AMSTAR 2's rule (more than one critical flaw). Item 7 'partial yes' fits: the 11 exclusions are cited with only a blanket reason. Item 2 'partial yes' is consistent with the article (prospective registration claimed, no deviation discussed), but its detailed notes rest on the PROSPERO record, which I could not read; if the registry record did not exist before the search started, 'partial yes' would still hold. Agree with the reasoning that the qualitative conclusion is robust to these problems.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right. The three gaps are all present in the text (abstract MD -0.49 vs Results SMD -0.70; Discussion 4.1 moving from two amineptine trials to a research strategy of methamphetamine-like longer-acting drugs; abstract's 'first comprehensive meta-analysis since 2008' framing). One small addition: Results 3.6 describes the continuous global-state effect as amineptine participants being 'more likely to improve', probability wording for a standardized mean difference.

missed: Market-withdrawal sourcing (relevant to cl_meth_withdrawal_medication): the review states the 1999 voluntary withdrawal of amineptine in Discussion 4.1 citing references 64 and 65, a 1996 report of two liver-injury cases and a 1998 report of amineptine and midazolam dependence. Both predate 1999, so the date itself is unreferenced in the review; the claim's 1999 date should be anchored to a primary regulatory or manufacturer source, or worded as 'according to the review'. The same group's 2020 review (siefried_2020, Results > Antidepressants, 1st paragraph) says only that amineptine was never FDA-approved and 'has been suspended in other jurisdictions', with no date or reference, so it does not corroborate 1999.

Safety reporting does not reconcile: Results 3.9 classifies 8 of 9 trials (one with adverse events by arm, three with prose descriptions, four with nothing; the 1997 amineptine trial is not mentioned), while Discussion 4.2 says four trials gave nothing and another four gave prose-only descriptions. Minor; it does not affect the statement that only one trial reported adverse events by arm.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with the overall 'low confidence' and with most item judgments, but items 11 and 12 use 'partial yes', which AMSTAR 2 does not offer for those items (partial yes exists only for items 2, 4, 7, 8 and 9; items 11 and 12 are yes / no / no meta-analysis). On AMSTAR 2's criteria item 11 would be 'yes' (rationale for pooling psychostimulants as a class is given in the Background, random-effects inverse-variance pooling, heterogeneity investigated with prespecified subgroups); if the editors instead treat the unexplained exclusion of Elkashef 2008 as an inappropriate method, item 11 becomes 'no', a second critical flaw, and the overall rating falls to critically low. Item 12 would be 'yes' (sensitivity analyses removing trials at high risk for selective reporting and incomplete outcome data were run, though only described as not changing the results). Item 3 'no' is defensible on a strict reading (no rationale given for restricting to RCTs). Item 4's note that the search ended within 3 months of submission could not be checked: the article-notes panel with the submission date is not in the saved text. Item 7 'no' (no list of excluded full texts) is the critical flaw and is correct.

interpretation_gap.note: The three gaps the card names are all in the text and correctly described. I would rate the gap 'substantial' rather than 'minor': the abstract and Conclusions state that psychostimulants as a class had no effect on sustained abstinence, while the abstinence analysis contained only bupropion and modafinil (no methylphenidate or dexamphetamine trial, i.e. 8 of the 17 trials' drugs untested on that outcome, four methylphenidate trials reporting fewer positive urines in Table 1), and 'no effect' is stated for intervals that allow roughly 6 points of benefit or harm (OR 0.65-1.45). The Discussion's body text is precise (it limits the null abstinence finding to modafinil and bupropion), so the gap is between the body and the abstract and conclusions. Senior-author call.

missed: Card field outcomes.multiplicity_correction says the six subgroup tests produced 16 subgroup estimates; recounted from Results, they produced 14 (abstinence by drug 2 and by frequency 2; retention by diagnosis 2, by drug 4, by frequency 2, by duration 2). Minor correction to the card text.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The four predictors dropped at p > .65 are correctly placed (Methods › 2.4 ¶3). The age-at-first-use statement (predictor in the 98-person preliminary analysis, not significant in the complete sample) is in Discussion (section 4) ¶9, the last paragraph before 4.1, not ¶7 (¶7 is about self-help and other drugs). The same paragraph number should be corrected in replication.timeline[0], which cites 'Discussion, 2nd and 7th paragraphs' (¶2 is right for the 57% figure; ¶9 for age at first use).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E is acceptable, and the domain set and judgments (confounding high; exposure measurement very high; selection, post-exposure interventions, missing data and outcome some concerns; reported result high; overall very high, not less severe than the worst domain) follow from the text. Two remarks for the senior author: (1) this is in substance a prognostic-factor study, and if a claim ever cites the continuing-care or treatment-duration association as an intervention effect, ROBINS-I would be the apt instrument for that result; (2) selection could defensibly be rated high for the descriptive relapse figures, since deaths and people not located (43% of sampled admissions) are plausibly linked to continued use, but some concerns is within reason for the predictor associations.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right. Points (1)-(4) are all supported by the text (Abstract vs Results › 3.2; Methods › 2.3; abstract omits point and re-abstinence results).

missed: Causal wording on treatment duration not flagged: Discussion ¶6 calls the HR 0.93 per month 'a positive effect of longer index treatment duration'. Time in treatment is plausibly a marker of in-treatment response (people still using tend to leave early; 36% used in the first month after discharge or at discharge), so this association is confounded by response, and the card's confounding note and interpretation gap do not name this for the treatment-duration result.

Discussion ¶5 suggests that 3-5-year remission after methamphetamine treatment may not be substantially worse than for other drugs, although the study has no comparison group of people treated for other drugs; this comparative statement rests only on informal comparison with other studies and is not noted in the interpretation gap.

key_findings_flagged.correction: NOT CHECKED rather than absent: this finding comes from the ClinicalTrials.gov record, which I could not open in this session (no web access). The article itself prints only the registration number NCT01888835 (Abstract, Trial Registration) and says the analysis model was prespecified with the protocol in Supplement 2 (not available). The registry dates, outcome history and the absence of posted results need a second check by someone with web access.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: NOT CHECKED on the registry side (ClinicalTrials.gov not accessible in this session). Article side confirmed: ages 18 to 65, anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months, and five named SSRIs permitted (Methods > Recruitment); four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs (Sensitivity Analyses).

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 domain judgments follow from the article: concealed off-site allocation and identical over-encapsulation (randomization low; the 85% vs 75% baseline positivity is compatible with chance); double-blind with intention-to-treat and a blinding check (deviations low); objective urine outcome (measurement low); 34-41% missing urines, more dropout on mirtazapine and a missing-completely-at-random primary analysis, with the positive-imputation sensitivity analysis only described in words (missing data some concerns, which I would not raise to high given that analysis reportedly stayed significant). Overall some concerns follows. One limit of my check: the 'selection of the reported result: low' judgment rests partly on the registry history, which I could not open; the article does say the model was prespecified, gives the registration number and puts the protocol in a supplement I could not read.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's content is right, but I would rate the gap 'substantial' rather than 'minor'. The Key Points, the part most often quoted, say mirtazapine is the first medication to show efficacy for methamphetamine use disorder in two independent trials (same team and population; abstinence not significantly different in this trial and most samples stayed positive) and that the sexual-risk reductions were consistent with the previous study, which the paper's own Discussion contradicts ('In contrast with the original study', with reductions only at 24 weeks, 3 of 6 measures at P = .04, no multiplicity correction). The Results text also calls the 24-week decline significant (RR 0.75, 0.56-1.00, P = .05). The Discussion and Limitations are measured, so the gap is between the body and the Key Points/abstract. Senior-author call.

missed: Results > Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph and the abstract describe the 24-week effect as a significant decline or a reduction, although its interval reaches 1.00 (P = .05); the card records the interval but not this wording, which matters for any claim that 'lowered' use at 24 weeks.

Overall weekly-visit completion is given as mean 66% with SD 47%, while the arm SDs are 32% and 31%; 47% is the SD of a binary visit indicator at 66% (computed over visits, not participants), so the overall SD is on a different basis from the arm SDs. Minor.

Funding and conflict-of-interest details on the card (NIH R01DA034527, NIDA R01DA031678; disclosures) could not be checked: the saved PMC text has no Article Information block. Treat these card fields as single-reader.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Attribution is narrower than the source. The review cites refs 13, 38 and 39 (Lappin 2017; Swor 2019; Zhu 2020) for younger age, better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, refs 13 and 39 for male predominance, and ref 39 (Zhu 2020) alone for lower hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher smoking; only the smoking difference is described as significant. Location (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶2-3) is right.

Content is exact (14 people with intravenous polysubstance use, 12 reporting methamphetamine, 1 exclusively; 4 fatal cases, 2 confirmed and 1 possible; monkeys; over 400 San Francisco deaths; 38 Australian fatal strokes; invoke rarely and with skepticism). It is in Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶4, counting text paragraphs. The card's ¶5 counts the Figure 2 legend as a paragraph; under that count a reader of the PMC page lands on the chronic-hypertension paragraph. The Brecht card in this batch counts text paragraphs only, so the convention should be standardised.

Content confirmed (no change in mean arterial pressure in small-animal studies, ref 65; white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors, ref 66). Location is Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶5 by text paragraphs; the card's ¶6 counts the Figure 2 legend.

Two fixes. (1) 'A larger fall from pre-stroke mRS' should read a larger worsening (increase) in mRS from pre-stroke to discharge; mRS rises with disability, so 'fall' reads as improvement. (2) The review cites that point to refs 38 and 39 together (Swor 2019 and Zhu 2020), not to Zhu 2020 alone. The rest is confirmed at Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶2 (n=41 vs n=61; the review itself misprints 'IV hypertensive agents', which the card rightly renders as antihypertensives).

Content confirmed (10/30 ventricular thrombi; QTc prolongation 27% of 158; 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation diagnosis; endocarditis even left/right with stimulants, 75% methamphetamine, versus 66% right-sided with opioids). Location is Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke ¶2-3 by text paragraphs; the card's ¶3-4 counts the Figure 5 legend.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The review's side is confirmed (Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5: up to 6.5 times, ref 9, Kaku & Lowenstein 1990). The comparison figures attributed to Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3: 6.5 ischaemic, 11.7 haemorrhagic) come from another paper and could not be checked in this reading.

Confirmed in this source: the sentence (ischemic pathophysiology ¶2, last sentence) cites refs 12 and 86-88, and the titles of 86-88 (a case of infarction with normal coronaries, an echocardiographic comparison, a study of binge administration) do not concern severity of use as a predictor. Not checkable here: that the corresponding sentence in Kevil et al. (2019) carries no citation, and that ref 88 is a rat study (its title names no species).

Confirmed in this source: the 2-5 times figure is worded as intracerebral haemorrhage (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1) with no intervals or adjustment, and ref 37's title concerns amphetamines or cocaine. Not checkable here: that both estimates are for haemorrhagic stroke generally, which rests on Lappin et al. (2017).

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design. The card is labelled narrative-review but is appraised with AMSTAR 2 (overall critically low). Under METHODS §5.3 a narrative review uses the editors' narrative-review checklist (instrument 'none-applicable'); scripts/rob_vocab.py flags this mismatch. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (no methods, search or criteria); appraisal of the cited studies = some concerns (informal appraisal of ICD-coded hospital cohorts, small aneurysmal-haemorrhage outcome studies, the 1970 vasculitis series and small route-of-use numbers, but the 2-5-fold, 6.5-fold and 86% figures are passed on without design, intervals or adjustment, one via an editorial); reliance on the authors' own work = low (only the two vignettes come from the authors' centre; no cited study is by the authors as far as the reference list shows); separation of evidence from speculation = some concerns (the body labels speculation, e.g. aneurysm growth and stroke risk after stopping, but the abstract and conclusion present 'clear risk', greater disability and a rising contribution to stroke in the young as findings); balance = some concerns (the body reports null and conflicting results, but the abstract and conclusion select the adverse readings). Overall = high, the worst domain. The substance of the card's AMSTAR reasoning (unsystematic, unappraised, every number to be taken from the primary source) carries over.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right. Each listed gap was found independently: 'clear risk' in the Conclusion; abstract on rising stroke rates in the young against Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5 (trends not specific to methamphetamine); greater disability in the Conclusion against no difference in discharge function or mortality (Therapeutic considerations & outcomes ¶2); 'case studies and series' in the abstract against the cohort and database studies in the body; the attribution in both vignettes.

missed: The abstract's statement that haemorrhagic stroke is the more common methamphetamine-related stroke type rests on the share of published case reports and series (over 80% haemorrhagic, ref 13). A share of published cases reflects what gets reported, not relative incidence, and the population studies cited give relative risks, not the haemorrhagic-to-ischaemic ratio among people who use methamphetamine. The card's interpretation gap does not flag this inference; monograph wording should not say 'more common' on this basis.

The withdrawal time course, which the abstract lists as one of the review's points, is not recorded: Diagnostic challenges and management ¶5 gives an early crash of 12-24 h, a withdrawal phase of 2-4 weeks and an 'extinction phase' of up to 6-12 months with cognitive and mood changes (refs 105-106, Acheson et al. 2023 and a 2009 Cochrane review). It is second-hand and should be traced to those sources before use, but the card should record it with that caveat.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Species are conflated in the second half. The beta-adrenoceptor antagonist result (propranolol, Albers & Sonsalla 1995, section 5.1.1 ¶2) is in mice; the sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, glucocorticoid and muscle calcium-release results (Makisumi 1998, section 5.1.1 ¶3) are in rats, and it is that rat series alone that supports the muscle-thermogenesis-under-glucocorticoid-permission reading. The first half (sympathectomy, and catecholamine-synthesis blockade working in rats but not mice and not at the raised ambient temperature) is confirmed at section 5.1 ¶2-3.

Content confirmed, locator off by one at the start: the serotonin-depletion result and the roughly 1 degree C greater response in mice genetically lacking brain serotonin are in section 5.1.3 ¶3, not ¶4 (¶4 is the plasma-serotonin paragraph, which the finding does not cover). The right span is 5.1.3 ¶3 and ¶5 to ¶8.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Confirmed: read from the author manuscript with the publisher's disclaimer, no printed pagination in the HTML, header date 14 May 2014. Not checkable here: that the print issue is October 2014; the saved text gives only the May 2014 date. Either way the citation year is 2014.

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design, as on sc_hemphill_2024. The card is labelled narrative-review but appraised with AMSTAR 2; METHODS §5.3 requires the editors' narrative-review checklist with instrument 'none-applicable', and scripts/rob_vocab.py flags the mismatch. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (none reported); appraisal of the cited studies = high (no appraisal of any kind, and no SYRCLE-type consideration of randomization, blinding or sample size in the animal literature that makes up nearly the whole evidence base); reliance on the authors' own work = some concerns (the sigma-receptor compounds offered in Table 2 as potential therapeutic options come from the corresponding author's programme, and two co-authors wrote several of the cited temperature-and-neurotoxicity studies); separation of evidence from speculation = some concerns (the body is explicit about what is unknown, but the abstract states two human generalizations the body does not support, and section 3.2 extrapolates to people prescribed stimulants without evidence); balance = low (a dedicated section on manipulations that did nothing, species differences and contradictory findings reported throughout). Overall = high, the worst domain. The card's AMSTAR reasoning carries over unchanged in substance, including that nothing here can anchor a quantitative claim.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is defensible and I agree, though a reader could argue for 'minor' because the gap is confined to two sentences. Both are in the abstract, both are about people, and both are contradicted in spirit by the body, which says the basis of the effect is largely unknown and unexplored; the abstract is what gets quoted.

missed: Table 1 files vasoconstriction and piloerection under 'activation of heat production mechanisms' for methamphetamine, whereas section 2 lists vasoconstriction and insulation as heat retention strategies and section 3.1 describes vasoconstriction as preventing heat dissipation. An internal inconsistency in the paper's own framing; it should be a reporting issue, since the table is the part most likely to be reused.

Several citations in section 3.1 do not support the statements they are attached to: the sentence that methamphetamine causes vasoconstriction cites an MDMA thermoregulation study in rats, an emergency-department study of chest pain, a myocardial infarction case report and an electrocardiographic study, none of which measured vasoconstriction; the saliva-spreading statement cites a general thermoregulation review. This belongs with the citation problems already recorded as reporting issue 3.

Section 4.1 is not represented in the key findings. Its substantive point for this card is the authors' statement that it is unclear whether maximum temperature elevation tracks peak plasma concentration or cumulative exposure, and that a metabolite can itself raise body temperature. That is the paper's own acknowledgement that no dose-temperature relation is established, which supports cannot_establish and should be anchored there (without the route and bioavailability figures, which are not needed for any claim).

Table 2 labels the serotonin-releasing drug discussed in section 5.1.3 ¶7 as a transporter inhibitor, while the text calls it an indirect agonist acting through several mechanisms and notes it also releases noradrenaline. A text-table inconsistency of the same kind as the spelling issues already listed.

Section 3.2 ¶3 extends the heat argument to children and adults treated for ADHD with amphetamine salts and to sport in hot weather. No evidence is offered, and this is a clinical extrapolation about a different substance and population; it should be flagged so that no monograph picks it up from this review.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Content confirmed exactly as quoted, but it is in Clinical Presentation ¶2, not ¶3. That section has only three paragraphs (acute and psychiatric presentation; trajectories and course, including these figures; cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease). The 5-year remission figure of up to 30% without treatment is in the same paragraph.

Content confirmed; the location is Clinical Presentation ¶3, not ¶4 (there is no ¶4). The sentence says methamphetamine 'is also present in 63% of opioid deaths', which the card's caveat to re-anchor in the MMWR report covers.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The author-manuscript title is confirmed from the saved text. The published title could not be checked: there is no browser in this session and the save contains no PubMed or publisher page. Reader 1's card says it was checked on PubMed; I can neither confirm nor contradict it.

risk_of_bias.note: Instrument and vocabulary are right: narrative-review with 'none-applicable' and the editors' checklist (METHODS §5.3), domain words from the low / some-concerns / high set, and overall 'high' equal to the worst domain. I reached the same five domain judgments independently. This is the one card of my five that applies the instrument the design calls for; sc_hemphill_2024 and sc_matsumoto_2014 use AMSTAR 2 for the same design and should be brought into line with this one.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right, and all six listed gaps check out: the abstract's doubling; the prescription-stimulant figure; 'results in significant long-term cognitive and neurological deficits' and 'possibly degenerative' against the body's own statement that the literature is debated and almost entirely cross-sectional; the Warburg passage resting on a cancer-biology reference; 'exercise helps to maintain abstinence' when the cited exercise studies measured craving, inhibitory control, depression and anxiety; and mirtazapine, which I confirmed appears nowhere in the text or reference list.

missed: The cardiovascular and cerebrovascular section (Clinical Presentation ¶3) has no key finding except the 63% opioid-death figure, although the card's can_establish offers the review as a pointer to that literature. Unrecorded statements from that paragraph: cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease as the most severe problems and leading cause of death; methamphetamine-related strokes rising, mostly in young men and primarily haemorrhagic; the associations with vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, atherosclerosis, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy; the cardiomyopathy and electrocardiogram descriptions; and the symptoms preceding death attributed to methamphetamine toxicity. These are the statements most likely to be cited from this review and they need anchors with their reference numbers.

'Leading cause of death' is sourced to a 10-year cohort of cardiovascular and stroke risk (reference 66). A cohort estimating risk does not establish what people who use methamphetamine most often die of; this is the same kind of inference the card flags elsewhere and should be in the interpretation gap.

The stroke sentence ('primarily hemorrhagic in nature', reference 67) rests on the share of published cases in a case-report review, not on relative incidence. The same inference is in sc_hemphill_2024, and both cards should carry the caveat so that no monograph states it as a fact about incidence.

Clinical Presentation ¶2 presents a 'gateway' statement (adolescent cannabis use raising the probability of initiating methamphetamine, via biological and social processes, from one longitudinal study) and the trajectory claim that transition from casual to compulsive use takes about 50, 60 and 85 days from a single sample. Both are causal-sounding generalizations from single studies; the card holds the 50/60/85-day figures in the exposure field but neither is flagged in the interpretation gap.

The 42.4% rise in deaths is cited to a report titled as covering cocaine and psychostimulants with abuse potential, 2003 to 2017, while the text reads 'cocaine, amphetamines, or both' for 2015 to 2016; this belongs with the construct mismatches in reporting issue 3.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Content confirmed; the span should be Neuropsychiatric complications ¶1-3, not ¶1-4. The 40% figure, the cited meta-analysis and the episodic-memory point are in ¶1, executive function in ¶2, fine-motor dexterity and the caudate-versus-putamen argument in ¶3. ¶4 is the anxiety, depression and psychosis paragraph, which this finding does not cover. The note is right that the 40% is cited to a study titled as concerning people with HIV.

Content confirmed; the right span is Neuropsychiatric complications ¶6-7. That section has seven paragraphs, so there is no ¶8: the symptom profile and the response to dopamine antagonists are in ¶6, and the amount-and-duration, variability and recurrence statements in ¶7.

Content confirmed; it is Neuropsychiatric complications ¶7, not ¶8. All four strands (family history, exacerbation in people with schizophrenia, unmasking, self-treatment and a shared neuronal substrate) are in that one long paragraph.

Content confirmed (26% or 40 of 150 with amphetamine addiction; 38% of 50 people addicted to cocaine; 3 hours a day on average; one person up to 14 hours; behaviour resembling the former occupation; sex differences; usually abates with abstinence; neither duration nor amount predicted it). The note is wrong on one point: the primary cocaine study is cited in the same paragraph, as reference 71 (a 2008 paper on cocaine addiction and punding by the same first author), where the review introduces punding in people who used cocaine. What is wrong is the citation at the sentence level: the 38% and the 3 hours carry reference 66 (the 2010 review) and the following sentences about 'this study' carry reference 67 (a 2009 review of dopamine dysregulation syndrome by a different group). So the figures are traceable, but not through the references attached to them.

Content confirmed; the span should be Parkinson's ¶2-3, not ¶2-4. The first three arguments (terminals rather than cell bodies, caudate rather than putamen, recovery of transporter binding after more than 12 months of abstinence) are in ¶2 and the vesicular-transporter argument in ¶3. ¶4 is the tobacco argument, which is finding 8.

Content is in Parkinson's ¶5, not ¶6 (the section has five paragraphs). Two further corrections: the review presents two studies involving the same group of patients, and the earlier age at symptom onset but not at diagnosis comes from the second of them, not from the telephone survey itself; and the interval is printed as 'confidence interval 1.6-41.4' without a level, so '95% CI' is the card's addition. Recomputed: the geometric midpoint of 1.6 and 41.4 is 8.1, consistent with the printed odds ratio of 8, and the card's caveat about its width is right.

Content confirmed (87-92% against 22%, and smoking inversely associated with Parkinson's disease, so possible partial protection); the location is Parkinson's ¶4, not ¶5. The note is right that both halves are second-hand and that the smoking proportions carry no sample, country or date.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The footnote is confirmed: the article originally appeared in the August 2011 issue of Neurologic Clinics, volume 29, number 3. The consequence (do not treat the two versions as independent sources) is right and important. The statement about how Kevil et al. (2019) cite it, including the page range, is outside this source and was not checked here.

Half of this stands and half does not. The citations are confirmed (references 43 and 46 for the 40%, reference 46 alone for the 70%), and so is the mismatch of setting: a 1969 British report and a 1967 description of amphetamine psychosis are not studies of admissions to methamphetamine treatment facilities. But 'methylamphetamine' in the 1969 title is an older name for methamphetamine, not a different substance, so the substance objection applies to the 1967 amphetamine source only. The issue should be reworded accordingly.

The sentence-level mis-citation is confirmed (references 66 and 67, both reviews, carry the figures). 'The underlying study is never cited' is wrong: it is reference 71, cited earlier in the same paragraph. The consequence should therefore be that the figures must be taken from that 2008 primary study, not that they are untraceable.

Confirmed in substance, with one amendment: the cocaine punding figure also carries a denominator (38% of 50 patients), so the exceptions are three, not two. Everything else is as stated, including the undated smoking proportions.

The first half is confirmed (author manuscript, print citation shown as Psychiatr Clin North Am 2013;36(2):261-275 with 11 April 2013, no page numbers in the text). The second half misreads the header: the line reads 'Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2014 Jun 1', which is the PMC availability date in 2014, not an issue date of June 2013. No June 2013 date appears in the saved text. The citation year is 2013 either way.

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design, as on sc_hemphill_2024 and sc_matsumoto_2014: a narrative review must use the editors' narrative-review checklist with instrument 'none-applicable' (METHODS §5.3), and scripts/rob_vocab.py flags AMSTAR 2 here. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (none reported, single author); appraisal of the cited studies = high (only the Parkinson's telephone survey is appraised, for small size and recall bias; several frequency figures come from sources whose population or substance does not match the statement); reliance on the authors' own work = low (two self-citations out of the references I could read, both used as background); separation of evidence from speculation = high (see 'missed': the Phineas Gage passage, the inference that people seen moving abnormally in public may be showing stimulant-induced choreoathetosis, and the Key Points treatment claim are presented alongside evidence); balance = some concerns (the Parkinson's section sets the hypotheses against each other; elsewhere the framing is categorical and causal). Overall = high. The card's AMSTAR reasoning carries over in substance: useful for clinical description and for the older literature, no figure citable from it.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right and every element checks out: the commentary's causal framing ('slowly damaging', 'preferentially causes'), 'devastating effects' in the Summary, the Key Points treatment claim with no trial behind it, the 40% figure traced to a study of people with HIV, and the Parkinson's section as the strongest part. The card's point that the body twice raises the possibility that deficits precede use, while the commentary does not, is confirmed (Neuropsychiatric complications ¶2 and the punding section).

missed: The review states near the end of the pharmacology section that the similarities between methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine and MDMA make the whole discussion of neurological complications largely translatable to those drugs. That is a substance-level generalization with nothing behind it, and it matters here because this encyclopedia files claims per substance and because several of the review's own figures are in fact about amphetamine or cocaine. The card records the sentence in the exposure field but does not flag it in the interpretation gap.

Two speculative passages are not recorded: the comparison of people who use methamphetamine to 'a modern Phineas Gage' with impaired memory leaving them 'doomed to repeat' past mistakes (Neuropsychiatric complications ¶1-2), and the suggestion in the choreoathetoid section that many homeless people seen moving abnormally in city streets may be showing stimulant-induced choreoathetosis. The second is an unevidenced inference about a vulnerable group; under METHODS §9 neither should be carried into any monograph, and the card should say so.

The history section attributes the 2006 fall in treatment admissions to the precursor legislation of the preceding year, on the authority of one review, and reports manufacture costs and earnings sourced to a university web page with a 2011 access date. A policy-effect claim from a single secondary source and figures from a web page that may no longer resolve should both be flagged as uncitable, alongside the United Nations annual-report web citation behind the 25, 14 and 11 million figures.

The review's vocabulary throughout is 'abuse', 'abusers', 'addicts' and 'epidemic'. The card paraphrases in person-first language, which is right, but a note that every paraphrase from this source must be reworded (METHODS §9) would help whoever drafts from it.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Signals were not confined to people with light baseline use: the Results (Antidepressants, 4th paragraph) also report a subgroup signal in male participants regardless of baseline use in Elkashef 2008 (higher proportion of MA-free weeks on bupropion), alongside the ORs 1.39 and 1.34 in men with low use and 1.27 in non-depressed women with low use; and Table 4 records a secondary finding in Heinzerling 2014 (more participants with negative urines on bupropion, with very low adherence). Suggested wording: 'signals were confined to post hoc, subgroup or secondary analyses (people with light baseline use, men) and to reduced cigarette smoking'.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with AMSTAR 2 and with critically low confidence: items 2 (no protocol) and 7 (no list of excluded studies) are unambiguous critical flaws. Four item-level points, none of which changes the overall rating: (a) item 4 should be 'no', not 'partial yes': AMSTAR 2's partial yes needs at least two databases, the search strategy and a justification of publication restrictions, and the English-only restriction is not justified; (b) item 9 should be 'no' on the article's evidence: the Methods list allocation of participants, blinding of participants or personnel, sample, completion, analysis, overstated conclusions and funding, but not allocation concealment or outcome-assessor blinding, which AMSTAR 2 requires even for partial yes; if the editors read 'allocation' as covering concealment, the trial-level judgments are only in the unseen supplement and the METHODS extension would give 'no information' with a provisional rating; (c) item 13 offers only yes or no in AMSTAR 2, so 'partial yes' is not available; I would record 'yes' (the Discussion and Conclusions attribute the absence of convincing results to small, biased samples and low completion), with the card's point about the named signals kept in the note; (d) items 11, 12 and 15 should be recorded as 'no meta-analysis' rather than omitted, so the domain list is complete.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right: the bottom line (no medication with convincing results) matches the evidence, and the gaps concern the ranking of 'signals'. One addition to gap (3): the pexacerfont trial not only failed to separate amphetamine from opioid results, Table 4 also reports no difference in withdrawal (AWQ), yet the Discussion names pexacerfont as a withdrawal candidate. The card's funding note (an author of the review is an author of the lisdexamfetamine trial protocol, reference 68) is a fair flag for the 'agonist therapies show promise' conclusion.

missed: Bupropion in men: the Discussion (Reduction in Use, 5th paragraph) attributes the signal in people with light baseline use or in men to Shoptaw 2008 (reference 60) alone, whereas the Results attribute the male-subgroup finding to Elkashef 2008 (reference 33). Minor misattribution; claims about a bupropion effect in men should cite Elkashef 2008 directly.

Amineptine market status: the review says amineptine was never FDA-approved and 'has been suspended in other jurisdictions' for liver toxicity and liability for non-medical use, with no date and no reference (Results > Antidepressants, 1st paragraph). Relevant to cl_meth_withdrawal_medication, whose 1999 withdrawal date rests on acheson_2023: this same-group review does not corroborate the date.
